newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Peace talks seen as North Korea's survival game.
newsitem.headline: Peace talks seen as North Korea's survival game.

text.p: North Korea has agreed to join four-nation peace talks in a shift of policy designed to hold the reclusive state together and pave the way for communism's first dynastic succession, analysts said on Thursday.
Threatened by famine and an economy in ruins, the Stalinist regime needs to mend its relationship with Western countries who could provide aid to help resolve its woes, they said.

The United States and South Korea on Wednesday announced that senior officials from North Korea and their countries would meet on Monday in New York in a bid to set in motion the peace process on the peninsula.

Seoul officials said the North had agreed to another meeting, tentatively scheduled for August and involving China as well as the three nations, to set an agenda for four-nation talks aimed at thrashing out a peace settlement to replace the fraying ceasefire that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
Yu Suk-ryul, senior fellow at the government-backed Institute of Foreign Affairs and National Security in Seoul, said acceptance of peace talks meant "a new start" in inter-Korean ties.
"China, as a key ally of the North, could play a constructive role by stopping Pyongyang seeking adventurist tactics," Yu said.
He noted that North Korea had previously insisted that any peace arrangement on the peninsula must be made directly by Washington and Pyongyang, excluding South Korea.
"The North wants to improve ties with the U.S. and Japan," said Lee Ho, South Korea's deputy unification minister.
Japan, along with South Korea, is the biggest potential donor for food and other kinds of aid as well one of the biggest potential investors in the country.
Pyongyang has asked Washington to remove North korea from a list of terrorist countries and lift economic sanctions which have been discouraging foreign investment.
"North Korea talks about 1.5 million tonnes of food aid from Seoul and Washington. It knows it should come to the peace table to secure large-scale assistance," Lee told Reuters.

South Korean civic groups have so far pledged 80,000 tonnes of food relief in addition to a Seoul government promise of $16 million in response to an appeal by the World Food Programme to try to resolve the current food crisis in the North.

Lee, who is in charge of analysing North Korea at the ministry, said all indications suggested Kim Jong-il would be formally anointed as general secretary of the ruling Workers' Party and state president, posts left vacant by the death three years ago of his father, the "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung.
July 8 marks the third anniversary and the end of the traditional three-year mourning period for the senior Kim. Analysts said this would clear the way for his son to assume the two titles.

Lee said Kim Jong-il faced the task of easing the food crisis before he could assume the presidency. "The starvation issue is not just a problem for this year. The North will certainly need outside food aid next year as well," he added.
Pyongyang's official media on Thursday quoted a top United Nations official as saying North Korea needed more food aid after visiting flood-hit district of Unpha, south of Pyongyang.

In a report monitored in Tokyo, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said visitng U.N. Under-Secretary General Yasushi Akashi "felt an urgent need for the international community to redouble humanitarian support to people in the flood-hit areas who are scarcely living on a little food".

Paik Hak-soon, fellow at the private think-tank Sejong Institute, said Seoul and Washington could offer bold concessions in return for North Korean commitments on security issues, including stopping missile exports and withdrawing offensive weapons and troops from the tense Korean border.
